---
title: "Missingness mechanisms"
---

Suppose an acceptability experiment asks whether a syntactic manipulation changes participants' ratings. On some trials, a participant gives no response before the trial ends. The response is absent, but the sentence condition, participant, and item remain observed. Can we analyze the available ratings as though the omissions had been generated by random coin flips?

We first need to name the measured response. An acceptability rating is a behavioral response that may reflect grammar, processing, meaning, plausibility, and task properties; it is not a direct observation of grammaticality ([Sprouse, *Acceptability judgments*](https://www.jonsprouse.com/papers/Sprouse%20-%20OHES.pdf)). Here the missing value is the intended rating for one participant--item trial.

A [**missingness mechanism**](https://academic.oup.com/biomet/article-abstract/63/3/581/270932) states how the probability of an observation pattern depends on observed and unobserved values. The three mechanisms below make different dependence claims. They do not describe three visual arrangements of blank cells. We use one partially observed response so that every conditioning variable can be named.

## Separating the observed and missing parts

Let $Y_i$ be the intended acceptability rating on trial $i$. Let $X_i$ collect variables observed whether or not the rating is supplied: sentence condition, item, participant, and any recorded pre-trial information. Finally, let $R_i=1$ when $Y_i$ is observed and $R_i=0$ when it is missing, following the [indicator convention](missingness-patterns.qmd).

The mechanism concerns

$$
P(R_i=1\mid X_i,Y_i),
$$

the probability that trial $i$ supplies a rating, given the always-observed variables and the rating that would have been recorded. The three labels restrict which of these named quantities that probability may depend on.

## Missing completely at random

Values are [**missing completely at random (MCAR)**](https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-MCAR.html) when the observation probability depends on neither observed nor unobserved measurements:

$$
P(R_i=1\mid X_i,Y_i)=P(R_i=1).
$$

Imagine that a software failure deletes each trial with the same probability, regardless of sentence condition, item, participant, or rating. Under this account, the available ratings are a random subset of the intended ratings.

MCAR is a strong claim. Failing to detect an association between missingness and an observed variable does not establish it. A finite dataset may provide insufficient information about the association, and the missing values cannot be checked directly.

## Missing at random

Values are [**missing at random (MAR)**](https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-MCAR.html) when observation may depend on observed measurements but does not additionally depend on the missing value after those measurements are conditioned on:

$$
P(R_i=1\mid X_i,Y_i)
=P(R_i=1\mid X_i).
$$

Suppose nonresponse is more common in one sentence condition, and condition is observed for every trial. Under an MAR account, condition, item, participant, or other variables in $X_i$ may change the probability that $Y_i$ is absent. Among trials with the same $X_i$, however, the unobserved rating does not further change that probability.

The name is potentially misleading. MAR does not say that blanks are scattered uniformly through the table. It permits visible and systematic missingness whenever that structure is explained by observed information.

## Missing not at random

Values are [**missing not at random (MNAR)**](https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-MCAR.html) when observation still depends on the unseen value after observed measurements have been considered:

$$
P(R_i=1\mid X_i,Y_i)
\neq P(R_i=1\mid X_i).
$$

Suppose participants are especially likely to withhold responses to sentences they would otherwise rate at the bottom of the scale. Even after condition, item, and participant information in $X_i$ has been considered, the unseen rating $Y_i$ may still predict whether it is recorded. This is an MNAR account.

The observed data generally do not identify this remaining dependence. Domain knowledge about the measurement process and sensitivity analyses are needed to ask how conclusions change under plausible MNAR departures.

## Working through one visible pattern

Consider six trials.

| trial | condition | item length | rating | observed |
|:--|:--|--:|--:|:--|
| t1 | baseline | 4 | 6 | yes |
| t2 | baseline | 7 | 5 | yes |
| t3 | baseline | 5 | 6 | yes |
| t4 | manipulated | 4 | 4 | yes |
| t5 | manipulated | 7 | missing | no |
| t6 | manipulated | 5 | missing | no |

All three baseline trials are observed, compared with one of three manipulated trials. The pattern is compatible with an MAR account in which observed condition predicts response. It is also compatible with an MNAR account in which ratings that would have been especially low are more likely to be withheld.

The observed proportions differ by condition in these six trials. But that descriptive fact does not prove that the population mechanism depends on condition, much less that the dependence is MAR rather than MNAR.

We can compute the visible proportions without claiming a mechanism.

```{r}
trials <- data.frame(
  condition = rep(c("baseline", "manipulated"), each = 3),
  item_length = c(4, 7, 5, 4, 7, 5),
  rating = c(6, 5, 6, 4, NA, NA)
)

trials$observed <- !is.na(trials$rating)

with(trials, table(condition, observed))
aggregate(observed ~ condition, data = trials, FUN = mean)
```

The proportions describe $P(R_i=1\mid\text{condition}_i)$ in this sample. They contain no direct information about the ratings for t5 and t6. Thus, the calculation can reveal a pattern relevant to MAR, but it cannot distinguish MAR from MNAR.

## Mechanisms can differ by level

An entire participant may be absent because recruitment failed; that person is outside the realized sample rather than a row with missing trial values. An enrolled participant may drop out before a later session. A recorded trial may lose samples because an eye tracker loses calibration. And a skipped word has an observed skipping outcome but no defined fixation duration. Assigning one mechanism to all four cases conceals different statistical objects.

The analysis should define the indicator and mechanism at the level where absence occurs. Participant absence, session failure, and trial absence may require different assumptions even when their blanks ultimately appear in one rectangular table.

## A plot cannot distinguish MAR from MNAR

A missingness plot alone cannot diagnose MCAR, MAR, or MNAR. The plot contains $R_i$, the observed $X_i$, and observed values of $Y_i$. The distinction between MAR and MNAR concerns the dependence of $R_i$ on $Y_i$ when that rating is unobserved, which the plot cannot display.

This limitation does not make pattern analysis useless. It can challenge MCAR, identify observed variables that should be retained, and guide sensitivity analyses. It cannot turn an unobserved dependence into an observed one.

::: {.callout-note title="Classify the claim"}
1. Under MCAR, may rating observation depend on the observed condition in $X_i$?
2. Under MAR, may missingness be visibly associated with sentence condition?
3. What additional dependence makes a mechanism MNAR?
4. Why can the six trial table not distinguish MAR from MNAR?
:::

A missingness mechanism restricts how observation may depend on named observed and unobserved variables. In this example, MCAR removes dependence on both $X_i$ and $Y_i$, MAR permits dependence on $X_i$, and MNAR retains dependence on the unseen rating $Y_i$. These assumptions determine what may follow when incomplete rows are deleted, which is the focus of [complete-case analysis](complete-case-analysis.qmd).
